title: Commercial orbital transportation from milestone-funded development to ISS cargo service
pressure: Space Shuttle retirement created an ISS cargo-transport gap while NASA sought to stimulate commercial capability instead of owning every development path through traditional procurement.
preExistingWorldModel: NASA traditionally contracted major systems under government-led requirements and oversight; commercial launch providers existed but routine ISS cargo service required new vehicles, rendezvous integration and service reliability.
candidateRoutes: milestone/pay-for-performance partnerships followed by service purchase
multiple commercial providers with ISS integration gates
observationsAndInstruments: NASA established COTS with a two-phase idea: assist industry demonstrations, then procure commercial ISS logistics services.
The 2006 strategy used funded Space Act Agreements and pay-for-performance milestones.
NASA added Orbital Sciences in 2008 and required vehicle/ISS integration and safety work.
The programme evolved into commercial resupply services with SpaceX Dragon and Orbital Cygnus rather than a single government vehicle.
decisiveTests: actual cargo delivery and return capability
ability to transition from development aid to purchased service
technicalOrScientificTransition: The engineering object changed from government-developed transport hardware toward an institutionally mediated capability market in which NASA specified integration/safety outcomes and purchased realized service.
rivalsAndFailures: Not every original COTS participant survived or completed its planned path.
Commercial status did not remove NASA integration/safety obligations.
diffusionAndScaling: Multiple providers and subsequent service contracts turned demonstrations into recurring logistics capability.
standardsAndInstitutions: NASA remained an authority for ISS interfaces and mission safety while suppliers owned substantial development/operation responsibility.
externalitiesAndCorrections: Cost, competition, reliability and provider continuity remained separate system properties.
secondOrderEffects: The procurement/realization model itself became reusable institutional knowledge for later commercial-space programmes.
sourceNativeSummary: COTS is as much an institutional invention as a vehicle story: milestone-bound co-investment, interface/safety gates and later service purchase changed how capability was produced and owned.
